nUsage: mcpjam cloud projects servers create|add [options]

Create a saved MCP server

Options:
 --project <id-or-name> Pro

ject name or ID
 --body <json> Server JSON body
 -h, --help display help for command
7:> Author test c
ases for your MCP server, run them across models, and gate pass/fail on deterministic assertions plus optional LLM-as-judge.\n23:A
group of cases plus the defaults they share: attached servers, models to run against, default assertions, judge config, and argum
ent-matching mode.\n27:One scenario you want to verify — a prompt (or a sequence of prompts), the tools you expect to fire, an opt
ional expected output, and the assertions that decide pass/fail.\n45:* **Prompt** — a user turn the model receives. The first prom
pt is always present; use **Add assertion or action** to add a second prompt for multi-turn cases.\n47:* **Assert** — an assertion
that grades the case.\n53:Use **Add assertion or action** to add an assertion, a second prompt, or an interact step. Each asserti
on row says what it checks, who wrote it, and what a miss does:\n56:* **Step N** — an assertion written as a step (what the CLI an
d the SDK produce). It is graded in place, at its position in the run, and is labelled by that position: a step-level \"no tool er
rors\" reads **No tool errors so far**, because it only sees the transcript up to that point. Editing one rewrites that step; it n
ever becomes a case-level assertion.\n57:* **This case** — an assertion you added here. It is graded once, over the finished trans
cript.\n60:The list reads as a checklist with progressive disclosure. An off row shows only its short name. Once on, clicking the
name opens an inline editor showing the full criterion, the **Required / Advisory** role control, and any editable fields (thresho
lds, match criteria). Multiple editors can stay open at once. An assertion that carries a number (such as a latency budget) shows
it under the name at rest.\n62:A row's **role** says what a miss does: **Required** fails the trial, **Advisory** shows the miss w
ithout failing it. The control appears when your deployment supports assertion policy; otherwise the role chip shows read-only wit
h a tooltip explaining why it cannot be changed — for example, when the assertion is inherited from the suite, or when the backend
does not yet support assertion policy.\n64:Because a failing required assertion halts the run, an assertion written as a step can
leave later assertions unrun. The trial column marks those **Skipped**.\n71:* **No tool should be called** — a negative case. It
passes only if the model called nothing. An assertion that requires a tool call contradicts this, and the spine says so.\n72:* **A
ny route** — the case names no route and is graded by its assertions. This is a normal positive case, and it is what most CLI- and
SDK-authored cases are.\n74:A brand-new case that asserts nothing at all must answer this question before it can be saved or run:
without an assertion, a goal sentence, or a named tool, it would pass vacuously.\n81:* **No sentence, but a route** — the judge g
rades against the expected route.\n101:The other tabs are unchanged: **Chat**, **Tool Calls** and **Trace** show the transcript, a
nd **Steps** shows execution order — now with the same assertion names the rest of the page uses and the reason under a failed ste
p.\n114:> A **negative case** is one you marked **No tool should be called**. Meta questions (\"what params does `search` take?\")
, conversational drift, and ambiguous prompts are the usual shape. A case that simply names no tool is *not* negative — it is grad
ed by its assertions.\n118:Click **History** in the trial header to open a list of past iterations. Selecting one freezes the left
form on that trial's snapshot — the exact steps, assertions, and settings that were in effect when it ran — so you can compare wh
at you see in the trace against what was authored at the time.\n161:Some widget interactions send a `ui/message` back to the host
(for example, a cart button that says \"Show my cart\") rather than calling a tool directly. During eval execution, these follow-u
p messages automatically drive a continuation model turn — the same way Playground handles them live. The resulting tool call (e.g
. `view-cart`) is attributed to the same `interact` step's turn, so a **Tool was called** assertion on that turn sees the call.\n1
63:This means an eval case can faithfully verify a full widget interaction sequence: prompt → widget renders → user clicks → model
reacts → tool fires → assertion passes.\n210:When an assertion is authored on an individual prompt turn it is evaluated against *
*that turn's slice** of the transcript — tool calls, assistant message, tool errors, and widget observations for that turn only. `
Token budget under N` is case-only because per-turn token usage is not reliably captured; all other assertions are turn-scopable.\
n217:> N` remains a valid assertion and keeps working wherever it is already authored,\n224:### Harness system tools in assertio
n dropdowns\n226:When a suite is configured to run under a harness host (such as Claude Code or Codex), the tool-name pickers in t
he case editor also offer the harness's native **system tools** — for example `bash`, `read`, `webSearch`, `WebFetch` — alongside
your MCP server tools. This lets you write assertions like **Tool was never called** for `bash` or **Tool was called with…** for `
read` without having to type the wire name by hand.\n228:System tools appear only in assertion pickers. They are not available in
pinned tool-call steps or widget-assertion \"View (tool)\" selects, because those require a tool that MCPJam can invoke directly.\
n236:* **partial** *(default)* — every expected key must be present and match; extra keys in the actual call are ignored. Best for
